pairs.a:
The timing question is what we are trying to settle. My eighteen-year-old son begins college this month, and he is having a left tympanoplasty to take out a highly unusual retained T-tube from his middle ear. We could have it done after his fall-semester exams in December while he recovers at home, or wait until next summer, when he has a far longer open period.

As a small child, he had the tube placed, but it shifted into the middle ear and somehow remained there for years. At present, his eardrum is fully intact, and the green tube can be seen through it. When he is well, his hearing is excellent: left SRT 0 dB, 100% word recognition, and a Type A tympanogram. Still, he suffers repeated, extremely painful left middle-ear infections, and he tends to get ill more often in winter.

A neurotologist/otologist with a focus on ear surgery thinks the retained tube is probably contributing to the infections and advises tympanoplasty for removal. He views it as a routine procedure and does not expect a CT to be necessary. He told us about one week away from work or school and no flying for two weeks.

I am mainly asking about everyday recovery, not whether he should undergo surgery:

* How long did your ear truly feel odd, full, or muffled after tympanoplasty?
* When did your hearing seem normal again?
* Did you have lasting tinnitus, pressure, popping, dizziness, or anything similar?
* How long before you felt completely normal?
* Did getting a cold during recovery create problems?
* If you could choose between having surgery during a 3–4 week winter break and waiting for a longer summer break, which would you choose?

I would especially welcome responses from anyone who had tympanoplasty or middle-ear surgery while starting with otherwise good hearing.

I have normal hearing test results, but I have constant tinnitus that sounds more like hissing/white noise. I feel like the hissing masks the sounds around me, so I often feel like everything sounds quieter than it should.

I have one Widex MOMENT hearing aid, and I got it not only for my tinnitus but also because I feel like I have difficulty hearing sounds clearly. The problem is, I honestly don’t notice much difference when I wear it compared to when I don’t.

I’m thinking about asking my audiologist to increase the amplification a little and see if that makes a difference. I want speech and environmental sounds to be more audible and closer to their natural level.

**One thing I noticed specifically with PureSound:** when I’m in a room with the AC on, the AC sometimes sounds like a **hair dryer/strong whooshing noise through the hearing aid. This only happens when I’m using PureSound.** When I’m not using PureSound, I don’t get that same hair-dryer-like sound.

Has anyone with normal hearing tests and tinnitus experienced something similar? Did increasing the amplification help? And has anyone noticed a difference between **PureSound and Universal**, especially with constant background sounds like AC?
pairs.b: My most recent audiogram lists thresholds between 0 and 25 dB HL, and my tinnitus is present throughout the day as a steady hiss in the left ear. In rooms with low background sound, I turn toward speakers and check the volume on devices. Speech and household sounds register at a lower level than the settings used by other people. I use one Widex MOMENT hearing aid in the left ear, fitted after tinnitus reports and repeated requests for repetition in group settings. During trials with the aid on and off in the same room, the device indicator shows activation, and my head turns toward nearby sounds at the same delay. I have an appointment with my audiologist and will request a 2 dB increase in amplification, followed by checks of speech and environmental sounds at the same distances. With PureSound selected, an operating AC unit produces a whooshing sound through the hearing aid, like a hair dryer. The same AC unit, at the same setting, does not produce that whooshing sound when PureSound is switched off and another program is used. I ask for responses from people with audiograms listing thresholds between 0 and 25 dB HL and tinnitus who have adjusted amplification, and for descriptions of PureSound compared with Universal in rooms with continuous background sound such as air conditioning.

pairs.a:
So, I was also skeptical of the aids, as I have been wearing aids for 35 years.  You get comfortable with aids, and your brain works hard to compensate - you don't realize how hard until there is a change (good or bad).  So, I went in and got a pair.  Not that I have $7K to throw around, but if I heard just 10% better, then that is an ROI that I can justify.  

I traveled from San Diego to NY to see my daughter, so I made an appointment.  I told myself that I could return them, so I didn't feel the $7K was at risk.   
  
I kept the aids due to their noise-cancellation and speech-focus in AI mode.  And I could tell that my brain-body was better, as I didn't even notice that my aids were in.  I also kept the aids, as my 10% did get better at Fortell's forte: hearing conversations in loud bars and restaurants.  They are way better than my Oticon aids (that cost me about the same).

If you are a hearing aid user, you know that correcting hearing loss is more of an art than a science, given the changing nature of hearing loss (dB changes across frequencies).  I feel Fortell is making it more of a science.  Their service model is basically remote for me, and to my surprise, it has worked out fine.  

I suggest writing down your top 10 problems and what would satisfy you in the hunt for new aids.  It sounds like proven studies between hearing aid manufacturers is a top priority.  Good luck in your journey.

I have worn hearing aids for thirty-five years. I traveled from San Diego to New York for an appointment with an audiologist. I purchased a seven-thousand-dollar pair of devices. After three weeks, I placed the devices back in their box and mailed them to the manufacturer. The company transferred the seven thousand dollars back to my bank account.

I stayed in New York with my daughter for two weeks. I visited three high-decibel bars and two restaurants. I wore the new devices during these visits. I also wore my Oticon devices on alternating days.

I carried a sound level meter and a notebook. I wrote down the decibel readings of the background noise and the speech frequencies. When I wore the new devices, the AI noise-cancellation mode reduced the ambient sound levels on my meter by three decibels. When I wore the Oticon devices, the ambient sound levels remained unchanged. I returned the new devices to the manufacturer.

I scheduled a remote appointment with the Fortell technician. The technician accessed my devices remotely and adjusted the frequency output. I watched the frequency response curve shift on my computer screen. I printed the graph and filed it in my folder.

I am now drafting a document for other hearing aid users. I am listing ten acoustic variables and the corresponding decibel measurements. I am compiling data from three different hearing aid manufacturers. I will post the document to the online forum.

I'm sorry to hear about your loss of hearing and I hope your situation improves!

One thing worth pointing out, though, is that a large majority of posters in this sub that do HBOT are doing it because they have ALREADY experienced hearing loss, and it's a well-established treatment just like steroids. The further loss of hearing from HBOT is documented in the literature but is found to be a very rare occurrence, and if you're already considering HBOT after hearing loss, it's probably not something that should sway someone away from treatment.
pairs.b: After my hearing test showed a lower threshold, I scheduled HBOT sessions at a clinic. In the online group, most people who post about HBOT have already recorded hearing loss before beginning treatments. Clinics administer HBOT under protocols comparable to steroid courses. Medical papers list cases in which hearing thresholds dropped further during HBOT. Those entries appear as a small proportion of the total documented cases. People with prior hearing loss continue to book HBOT appointments, and the recorded incidence is included in the clinical information they receive.
